summary: This RFC specifies fully-specified FEC schemes for Raptor and RaptorQ codes and how they apply to reliable delivery of media streams within the FEC Framework. These codes send extra repair symbols along with the original ones.

plainLanguage.summary: You send a puzzle with a few spare pieces, so even if some get lost, the picture can be put back together.

subtitle: Six protocols for adding spare repair symbols to media streams

tldr.problem: Media streams sent over networks can lose packets, making video or audio incomplete. Resending lost packets creates long delays that live broadcasts cannot tolerate.
tldr.mechanism: Raptor and RaptorQ codes generate a small number of repair symbols mathematically derived from the original source packets. These repair symbols are sent separately; if packets are lost, received repair symbols can recover the missing data.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can reconstruct lost packets without asking the sender to retransmit, eliminating wait time. The codes offer near-optimal protection with low computational cost and are used in MBMS and DVB systems.

today: RFC 6681 is a Proposed Standard and defines the FEC schemes that are used in 3GPP MBMS and ETSI DVB standards for reliable media delivery. These schemes remain in active use for broadcast and multicast video streaming where the low processing overhead and near-optimal recovery properties of Raptor and RaptorQ are valuable.

sections.title: The Problem of Packet Loss in Media Delivery
sections.content:
When audio or video travels over networks like the Internet, packets sometimes get lost. The receiver can ask the sender to send them again, but this delay makes live broadcasts unacceptable.

The RFC specifies Raptor and RaptorQ codes, which are systematic codes: they send some original packets, then add extra repair symbols that let a receiver recover any missing original packets. The key advantage is that repair data can be calculated in advance and sent without waiting to discover which packets were lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine mailing puzzle pieces to someone. Some might get lost. You could send duplicates, but that takes time. Better: send a few special pieces that work with any missing pieces to complete the puzzle.

sections.title: How Raptor and RaptorQ Work
sections.content:
Raptor and RaptorQ are fountain codes: from a group of source packets called a source block, one can generate an unlimited number of repair symbols. The codes have two key properties:

  • They are systematic: source packets are sent unchanged, and repair symbols are computed from them.
  • They offer near-optimal recovery: the original source block can be recovered with very high probability from a set of symbols (source and repair) only slightly larger than the original number of source symbols.

RaptorQ is more powerful: the original source block can often be recovered from exactly the same number of symbols received as were originally sent. Both codes compute at low cost, making them practical for video streaming and broadcast applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The code is like a magic recipe: take any subset of the pieces you receive (original or spare) that is just slightly bigger than the original number, and you can magically rebuild all the original pieces.

sections.title: Six FEC Schemes: The Framework
sections.content:
The RFC defines six Fully-Specified FEC Schemes for use within the IETF FEC Framework. Each scheme specifies exactly how source symbols are constructed, how repair symbols are generated, and how payloads are formatted. The schemes split into three pairs based on how source packets are identified:

  • Schemes 1 and 2 (arbitrary packet flows): Applied to any packet sequence. The sender adds an explicit FEC Payload ID to each source packet so the receiver can identify which packet is which. Scheme 1 uses Raptor codes, Scheme 2 uses RaptorQ.
  • Schemes 3 and 4 (optimized for small blocks): Restrict source block sizes to a predefined set (101, 120, 148 symbols for Raptor; specific values for RaptorQ). This allows both encoder and decoder to precompute and embed operation sequences, reducing computational overhead.
  • Schemes 5 and 6 (sequenced flows): Designed for source packets that already have a sequence number (such as RTP packets). Because the sequence number is already present, no explicit FEC Source Payload ID needs to be added, maintaining backwards compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six different ways to set up the magic recipe, depending on whether your packages already have labels, whether you want to optimize for small shipments, or whether your packages already have sequence numbers.

sections.title: Symbol Construction and Payload IDs
sections.content:
All schemes follow a common procedure to construct source symbols from incoming packets. The sender takes each Application Data Unit (ADU, typically a packet payload) and wraps it in metadata: the source flow identifier, the ADU length, and padding to align to symbol boundaries. These are packed into symbols of a fixed size (the encoding symbol size T).

Each source packet is assigned an Encoding Symbol ID (ESI), the index of its first symbol in the source block. Each source block is assigned a Source Block Number (SBN).

For arbitrary packet flows, two payload ID formats are supported: Format A uses 16 bits for SBN and 16 bits for ESI, suitable for streams with many small blocks. Format B uses 8 bits for SBN and 24 bits for ESI, better for streams with fewer large blocks. Repair packets carry the source block number, repair symbol indices, and the source block length so receivers can identify which symbols were lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece gets labeled with which block it belongs to and its position in that block, so the receiver knows which pieces have arrived and which are missing.

sections.title: Protection Methods and Use Cases
sections.content:
The FEC protection operation is independent of the type of media. In all schemes, the sender determines a source block (a set of packets), constructs source symbols, applies the Raptor or RaptorQ FEC encoder to generate repair symbols, and sends repair packets separately from source packets—either over UDP or, for schemes used with RTP, within RTP streams.

At the receiver, if all source packets arrive, the repair packets are discarded and no FEC processing is needed. If source packets are missing, the repair packets enable recovery: the FEC decoder uses any combination of received source and repair symbols to reconstruct lost source packets.

The RFC notes that these schemes are equivalent to those defined in 3GPP MBMS (Multimedia Broadcast/Multicast Service) and ETSI DVB (Digital Video Broadcasting) standards when used with Raptor codes. This ensures interoperability with existing deployed systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Send the puzzle and some spare pieces separately. If all pieces arrive, ignore the spares. If some are missing, use the spares to fill in the gaps.

sections.title: Configuration and Deployment
sections.content:
Each FEC Scheme instance requires configuration information including the Maximum Source Block Length (MSBL, the largest number of source symbols in a block), the encoding symbol size T, and the payload ID format. These parameters are signaled through the FEC Framework Configuration Information.

For Schemes 3 and 4 (optimized), the MSBL must be chosen from a small precomputed set. For Scheme 3 (Raptor), valid values are 101, 120, 148, 164, 212, 237, 297, 371, 450, 560, 680, 842, 1031, 1139, and 1281 symbols. For Scheme 4 (RaptorQ), the valid values are those supported by the RaptorQ specification.

The RFC specifies how to use these schemes with RTP and Session Description Protocol (SDP) for signaling. It also addresses congestion control: implementers should refer to the FEC Framework guidance on adjusting repair flow rates based on network conditions. The marker bit in RTP headers indicates the last repair packet for each source block, helping receivers know when to attempt decoding.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to agree on how big the blocks are, how big each piece is, and how to label them. Then you can send the puzzles and spare pieces in real time without waiting.
